## Final hypothesis (natural-language answer)

**Individuals with a criminal record (operationalized as `ever_jailed == 1`, n=289) had significantly lower wealth than those without (n=11,724) in ALL three measured years — 1985, 1990, and 1996** — and this holds under every significance-testing approach, both raw and after multiple-comparison correction.

- **1985**: median wealth $720 (jailed) vs $3,600 (not jailed); Hodges–Lehmann shift $1,260; mean difference $17,157; Cliff's delta −0.218. One-sided Mann–Whitney **p ≈ 8.0×10⁻¹¹** (BH-FDR p ≈ 8.0×10⁻¹¹; Holm p ≈ 8.0×10⁻¹¹).
- **1990** (largest gap): median $0 vs $10,500; HL shift $7,850; mean difference $57,598; Cliff's delta −0.420. **p ≈ 3.9×10⁻³⁵** (BH-FDR p ≈ 1.2×10⁻³⁴; Holm same).
- **1996**: median $0 vs $8,500; HL shift $6,000; mean difference $85,063; Cliff's delta −0.351. **p ≈ 4.6×10⁻²⁶** (BH-FDR p ≈ 7.0×10⁻²⁶; Holm p ≈ 9.3×10⁻²⁶).

Effect sizes are small-to-moderate in rank terms (Cliff's delta −0.22 to −0.42) but translate to large dollar/median gaps, with the jailed group's median at or near zero in 1990 and 1996. The rank gap is largest in 1990, then 1996, then 1985; the mean (not-jailed − jailed) gap grows monotonically over time ($17.2k → $57.6k → $85.1k) alongside overall wealth growth.

**All robustness checks corroborate the same three years**: (1) two-part decomposition — the jailed group has a significantly higher share with wealth ≤ 0 in every year (45.0% vs 31.8% in 1985; 56.8% vs 29.2% in 1990; 63.0% vs 40.4% in 1996; chi² p = 2.1×10⁻⁶ / 5.4×10⁻²⁴ / 1.3×10⁻¹⁴, Fisher OR 1.75 / 3.18 / 2.51) AND significantly lower log₁₀ wealth among positive-wealth respondents (Welch one-sided p = 7.2×10⁻⁸ / 1.3×10⁻¹⁵ / 4.7×10⁻¹⁵); (2) inverse-hyperbolic-sine covariate-adjusted OLS including race and sex — the jail coefficient remains large, negative, and significant in all years (−0.49 / −1.45 / −1.63 in asinh($/1000) units; one-sided p = 2.3×10⁻⁵ / 2.3×10⁻²² / 1.4×10⁻²²), so the gap is not merely a race/sex composition artifact; (3) after dropping 1,899 full-row duplicate rows (n=10,114), all three years remain significant under BH-FDR (p = 1.6×10⁻¹³ / 6.3×10⁻⁴² / 4.9×10⁻³⁰). No sensitivity analysis flips any conclusion.

**Recommended headline**: lower wealth among criminal-record individuals was found in **every wealth year present in the data (1985, 1990, 1996)**, with the largest and most extreme gap in 1990.

payload.hypothesis: Individuals with a criminal record (ever_jailed==1; n=289) had significantly lower wealth than those without (n=11,724) in every wealth year measured — 1985, 1990, and 1996 — confirmed by one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p=8.0e-11 / 3.9e-35 / 4.6e-26), all significant after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR and Holm correction across the three year-tests, and robust to two-part decomposition, race/sex-adjusted IHS OLS, and deduplication. The largest rank gap was in 1990 (jailed median $0 vs not-jailed $10,500; Hodges-Lehmann shift $7,850; Cliff's delta -0.42), followed by 1996 (median $0 vs $8,500; delta -0.35) and 1985 (median $720 vs $3,600; delta -0.22).
payload.workflow: 1) Described groups and missingness (12,013x6, zero missing; 2.41% jailed). 2) One-sided Mann-Whitney U per year (jailed < not-jailed) on raw wealth; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR + Holm across the 3 year-tests (verified against statsmodels.multipletests). 3) Effect sizes: Hodges-Lehmann location shift, median difference with 4,000-iteration bootstrap 95% CI, mean difference, Cliff's delta/rank-biserial. 4) Robustness: two-part decomposition (chi2/Fisher on share wealth<=0; Welch t on log10 among positives), inverse-hyperbolic-sine covariate-adjusted OLS with race and sex, and BH-corrected tests after dropping full-row duplicates. 5) Reconciled raw vs corrected p-values and across all approaches: all three years significant everywhere; no analysis flips any conclusion. All results saved to artifacts/.
